skill.trigger: When comparing serial chest images where one shows a distinct focal abnormality and another appears normal or shows the same stable finding.
steps: Inspect the 'abnormal' image for the presence of a tubular opacity and hyperlucency.
Compare this to the baseline or follow-up image to assess for change in size or density.

If the morphology is characteristic of a congenital anomaly (like bronchial atresia), prioritize the option describing stability/persistence over options suggesting resolution or progression, even if the comparison image appears normal (which may represent a different anatomical slice or a prior normal study used for contrast rather than disease evolution).

skill.trigger: When evaluating a chest X-ray for tracheal abnormalities and associated parenchymal lung disease, specifically to distinguish between well-defined nodular opacities and ill-defined infiltrates.
steps: Inspect the tracheal caliber on the frontal view; confirm tracheomegaly if the transverse diameter significantly exceeds normal limits (e.g., >25 mm in men, >21 mm in women) or appears markedly widened relative to the thoracic inlet.
Systematically scan the lung fields to locate opacities, paying attention to their margins and distribution.

Differentiate 'well-defined' from 'ill-defined' opacities: Well-defined opacities have sharp, distinct borders suggesting nodules, masses, or cysts (often seen in bronchiectasis or specific infections), whereas ill-defined opacities have hazy, fuzzy borders suggesting alveolar filling, edema, or active inflammation.
Verify the laterality (left vs. right) and vertical zone (upper, middle, lower) of the identified findings to ensure accurate anatomical localization.

skill.trigger: When describing the specific anatomical distribution of pulmonary findings on a chest radiograph to differentiate between similar diagnostic options.
steps: Identify the primary airway abnormality (e.g., tracheal widening) as the anchor point for the syndrome.
Divide the lungs into zones (upper, mid, lower) and sides (left, right) using anatomical landmarks like ribs and fissures.
Characterize the texture of opacities in each zone: look for discrete, rounded densities (nodular/well-defined) versus reticular, linear, or hazy patterns.

Correlate the side and zone of the nodular/well-defined opacities with the side and zone of the linear/reticular opacities to form a complete spatial description (e.g., 'right lower lobe nodules' vs 'left base linear opacities').

skill.trigger: When evaluating a prenatal ultrasound showing a fetal thoracic mass to determine the specific type of Congenital Cystic Adenomatoid Malformation (CCAM/CPAM).
steps: Assess the cyst morphology and size within the echogenic lung mass: distinguish between macrocystic (single or multiple large cysts >5 mm, typical of Type I), microcystic (uniformly echogenic with tiny cysts <5 mm, typical of Type III), and mixed/small cystic patterns (multiple small cysts generally <2 cm, typical of Type II).

Differentiate Type II from Type I by confirming the absence of dominant large cysts (>5-10 mm) and differentiating from Type III by identifying visible discrete cystic spaces rather than a solid-appearing echogenic mass.

Correlate the imaging phenotype with clinical status: recognize that asymptomatic presentations without hydrops typically support conservative postnatal management regardless of the specific subtype, whereas hydrops or severe respiratory compromise would necessitate intervention.

skill.trigger: When evaluating a fetal thoracic mass on ultrasound to determine the specific subtype of Congenital Cystic Adenomatoid Malformation (CCAM/CPAM).
steps: Assess the echotexture and cyst morphology of the lung lesion.
Identify if the mass contains single or multiple large cysts (>2 cm) with thin septations (indicative of Type I).
Identify if the mass consists of numerous small, uniform cysts (<2 cm) creating a 'honeycomb' appearance (indicative of Type II).
Identify if the mass appears as a solid, homogeneous, highly echogenic area without distinct macroscopic cysts (indicative of Type III/microcystic).

skill.trigger: When identifying the specific lobar location and spatial position of a pulmonary nodule or vascular lesion on a coronal chest CT.
steps: Identify the hyperdense lesion and determine its vertical level relative to the heart (e.g., mid-lung zone corresponds to the middle lobe or lingula).
Assess the horizontal position relative to the mediastinum and heart border; a lesion separated from the cardiac silhouette by aerated lung is 'lateral', whereas one abutting the heart is 'medial'.
Evaluate adjacent airways for signs of mass effect, such as displacement or compression, to distinguish between options describing different anatomical relationships.

skill.trigger: When assessing cardiac size on a PA chest radiograph to determine if cardiomegaly is present alongside other pathology.
steps: Measure the maximum transverse diameter of the cardiac silhouette and compare it to the maximum internal transverse diameter of the thorax at the level of the diaphragm.
Identify cardiomegaly if the cardiothoracic ratio exceeds 0.5 (50%) on a standard PA projection.

Distinguish true cardiomegaly from apparent enlargement caused by AP projection or poor inspiration by verifying the 'PA ERECT' marker and ensuring the diaphragm is at an appropriate level (e.g., 9th-10th posterior rib).

skill.trigger: When evaluating a thoracic mass on a lateral chest X-ray to determine if it originates from the lung parenchyma or extrapulmonary structures (e.g., pleura, chest wall, mediastinum).
steps: Inspect the interface between the mass and the adjacent chest wall (ribs/sternum/spine) or mediastinum on the lateral projection.

Assess the angle formed by the mass margin and the surface it abuts: an obtuse angle (>90 degrees) with a broad base suggests an extrapulmonary origin, whereas an acute angle (<90 degrees) typically indicates a pulmonary parenchymal origin.
Evaluate the margins: well-circumscribed, smooth borders favor extrapulmonary lesions (like pleural tumors), while irregular or spiculated margins often suggest primary lung malignancy.

skill.trigger: When evaluating a focal hyperdense opacity within the airways on CT to determine its composition and etiology.
steps: Place a Region of Interest (ROI) measurement tool directly over the hyperdense object within the bronchus.

Compare the measured Hounsfield Unit (HU) value against standard tissue densities: metallic foreign bodies typically exhibit very high attenuation (>400 HU), whereas mucous plugs, blood, or soft tissue masses generally range between 20-80 HU.
Distinguish foreign body obstruction from mucous plugging by confirming the presence of metallic-density attenuation rather than soft-tissue density.

skill.trigger: When evaluating a smooth, cap-like opacity at the lung apex on a chest radiograph to distinguish benign pleural thickening from malignant or infectious etiologies.
steps: Assess the morphology of the apical opacity: Benign apical caps typically present as smooth, symmetric, and thin (<5mm) soft tissue densities capping the apex without a discrete mass effect.

Evaluate for aggressive features: Look for lobulated margins, invasion of adjacent ribs or vertebrae, cavitation, or associated lymphadenopathy, which would suggest Pancoast tumor or active tuberculosis.
Check for ancillary signs of chronicity: Identify evidence of prior inflammation such as calcification or rib deformity, which supports a diagnosis of benign scarring over acute pathology.

skill.trigger: When evaluating a chest X-ray for a suspected apical lung mass or Pancoast tumor.
steps: Inspect the lung apices systematically for any soft tissue opacity or mass effect.
Trace the posterior ribs (specifically the 1st and 2nd ribs) adjacent to any apical opacity to check for cortical destruction, erosion, or complete absence of the rib bone.
Examine the contralateral apex for subtle pleural thickening or asymmetry compared to the affected side.

skill.trigger: When evaluating a patient with recent vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty presenting with acute respiratory symptoms or intraoperative hemodynamic changes (e.g., drop in end-tidal CO2).
steps: Inspect chest CT images (specifically axial lung windows) for hyperdense, radiopaque material within the pulmonary arterial tree that matches the density of bone cement (polymethylmethacrylate).

Distinguish cement embolism from thrombotic pulmonary embolism by noting that cement appears significantly brighter (metallic/calcium density) than soft-tissue thrombus and often presents as linear or branching structures conforming to vessel lumens.

Differentiate from vascular calcification by confirming the material is located intraluminally within the pulmonary arteries rather than in the vessel walls, and correlating with the procedural history.

skill.trigger: When distinguishing between lung lobes or segments on axial chest CT to validate a reported finding.
steps: Identify the slice level relative to key structures (e.g., trachea, carina, heart); upper slices showing the trachea and great vessels correspond to upper/middle lobe anatomy, while lower slices showing the ventricles correspond to lower lobes.
Check for the presence of fissures or specific bronchovascular patterns that define lobar boundaries (e.g., the horizontal fissure for the right middle lobe).
Reject options describing findings in lobes not visible at the current slice level or inconsistent with the visible anatomy (e.g., ruling out left lower lobe pathology when viewing the upper thorax).

skill.trigger: When evaluating a chest X-ray series showing rapid progression from bilateral opacities to dense consolidations followed by complete radiological resolution within a short timeframe (e.g., two weeks).
steps: Compare the initial imaging (showing bilateral opacities) with subsequent images demonstrating rapid evolution into dense, confluent consolidations.
Verify the presence of complete or near-complete radiological clearance in follow-up imaging obtained within a short interval (approx. 2 weeks).

Correlate this specific temporal pattern—rapid worsening to consolidation followed by swift resolution—with alveolar hemorrhage syndromes (such as Weil Syndrome/Leptospirosis), distinguishing it from bacterial pneumonia (which typically resolves slower and requires antibiotics) or viral pneumonias (which often leave residual interstitial markings).

skill.trigger: When evaluating pulmonary opacities on a chest X-ray to determine etiology based on margin definition and anatomical distribution.
steps: Inspect the borders of the opacity to distinguish between well-defined (sharp, distinct margins suggesting consolidation or mass) and ill-defined (hazy, patchy, or ground-glass appearance suggesting interstitial or early alveolar process).
Localize the opacity vertically within the lung fields (apex, mid-zone, or base/lower zone) by referencing rib levels and the diaphragm contour.

Correlate the combination of ill-defined margins and lower/mid-zone predominance with viral pneumonias (e.g., COVID-19), whereas well-defined lobar opacities typically suggest bacterial pneumonia, and apical opacities suggest chronic conditions like TB or malignancy.

skill.trigger: When evaluating treatment response by comparing baseline imaging (e.g., CXR) with follow-up cross-sectional imaging (e.g., CT) to determine disease progression or resolution.
steps: Identify the specific pathology in the baseline image (e.g., bilateral interstitial infiltration on CXR).
Identify the specific pathology in the intermediate/follow-up images (e.g., multiple pulmonary nodules, potentially cavitary, on CT).
Examine the final follow-up image for the presence or absence of the previously identified lesions.

Correlate the visual change (specifically complete resolution/absence of nodules) with a successful treatment response, distinguishing it from options suggesting size increase, stability, or partial response.

skill.trigger: When evaluating a chest X-ray with multiple pulmonary nodules to determine the specific zonal distribution and morphological characteristics for differential diagnosis.
steps: Assess the vertical distribution of nodules by comparing density in the upper zones (above the anterior 2nd rib) versus the lower zones (below the hilum/diaphragm level).
Evaluate nodule margins (well-defined vs. ill-defined/spiculated) and check for internal calcification.

Correlate findings: Lower zone predominance with well-defined, non-calcified nodules suggests necrotizing sarcoid granulomatosis; upper zone predominance suggests tuberculosis; uniform distribution suggests typical sarcoidosis.

skill.trigger: When evaluating a chest X-ray for signs of blunt aortic injury or mediastinal pathology.
steps: Assess the width of the superior mediastinum relative to the thoracic diameter (widening is typically >8 cm or >25% of thoracic width at the level of the aortic knob).
Inspect the costophrenic angles and lung bases for the 'deep sulcus sign' (an abnormally deep, lucent costophrenic angle) which indicates a subpulmonary pneumothorax.
Distinguish blunt aortic injury from isolated pneumothorax by confirming the presence of mediastinal widening alongside basal lucency, rather than tracheal deviation or normal mediastinal contours.

skill.trigger: Evaluating a chest X-ray in the context of blunt trauma or crush injury to assess for vascular injury.
steps: Assess the mediastinal width by comparing the transverse diameter of the mediastinum at the level of the aortic knob to the thoracic diameter; widening is typically defined as a ratio greater than 0.25.
Inspect the contour of the aortic arch and descending aorta for indistinctness, obscuration, or abnormal bulging at the isthmus.

Distinguish traumatic widening from normal pediatric variants (e.g., prominent thymus) by noting that trauma-related widening often presents with ill-defined borders and loss of normal fat planes, whereas a thymus typically has smooth, well-defined margins and may show a 'sail sign'.

skill.trigger: Evaluating a chest X-ray in the context of blunt thoracic trauma (e.g., crush injury, MVA) to distinguish between pulmonary parenchymal injury and vascular/diaphragmatic trauma.
steps: Assess lung fields for diffuse, patchy, non-segmental airspace opacities that do not conform to anatomical lobes or vascular distributions, which are characteristic of pulmonary contusions.

Evaluate the mediastinal contour specifically for widening (>8 cm at the level of the aortic knob), loss of the aortopulmonary window, or deviation of the trachea/NG tube to rule out blunt aortic injury.
Inspect the hemidiaphragms for abnormal elevation, discontinuity, or intrathoracic herniation of abdominal contents to exclude traumatic diaphragmatic rupture.
Check costophrenic angles and lung bases for meniscus signs or layering densities to identify pleural effusions/hemothorax rather than pure parenchymal consolidation.

skill.trigger: Evaluating a chest X-ray in the context of high-energy blunt thoracic trauma (e.g., crush injury, deceleration) to identify signs of vascular injury.
steps: Assess the superior mediastinum for widening (typically >8 cm at the level of the aortic knob) and check for loss of definition or obscuration of the aortic knob contour.
Look for secondary signs such as deviation of the trachea or nasogastric tube to the right, depression of the left main bronchus, or apical capping (pleural cap).

Distinguish blunt aortic injury from other causes of mediastinal widening (like hematoma or lymphadenopathy) by correlating the specific location (isthmus) and mechanism; recognize that simple pneumothorax or isolated rib fractures do not explain significant mediastinal contour abnormalities.

skill.trigger: When evaluating a chest X-ray with focal pulmonary nodules to determine precise anatomical localization and distinguish specific patterns from diffuse or pleural disease.
steps: Inspect the frontal view for discrete nodular opacities and assess their relationship to adjacent mediastinal structures.
Identify silhouetting of the right heart border to localize a nodule to the right middle lobe.
Identify opacities visible behind the cardiac shadow (retrocardiac) on the frontal view and confirm posterior location on the lateral view.
Distinguish this specific dual-location pattern (RML + retrocardiac) from options describing diffuse miliary distribution, perihilar infiltrates, cavitary lesions, or pleural effusions.

skill.trigger: When distinguishing between primary ciliary dyskinesia manifestations (Kartagener's) and other causes of bronchiectasis or consolidation.
steps: Check for the specific triad components: situs inversus, chronic sinusitis (often not visible on CXR), and bronchiectasis.
Differentiate 'situs inversus' (complete mirror image: right heart + left stomach) from isolated 'dextrocardia' (right heart only) or normal anatomy.

Select the option describing the anatomical reversal (e.g., left-sided liver/right-sided heart) as the supporting finding for Kartagener's over options describing only lung parenchymal disease without mentioning the positional anomaly.

skill.trigger: When evaluating a chest X-ray in a patient with fever, dyspnea, and cough to distinguish opportunistic infection patterns from other chronic lung diseases.
steps: Inspect the lung fields for bilateral, diffuse reticulonodular or ground-glass opacities.
Assess the distribution of opacities, specifically checking for a predilection for the lower lung zones.

Differentiate this pattern from upper-lobe predominant diseases (e.g., TB, Alpha1-Antitrypsin deficiency) and airway-centric diseases like COPD or Kartagener's syndrome (which typically show bronchiectasis or situs inversus).
Correlate the finding of diffuse lower-zone interstitial opacities with immunosuppression-related etiologies such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

skill.trigger: When determining the laterality and compartment of a mediastinal mass on an axial CT scan.
steps: Identify the patient's right side as the viewer's left side of the image, consistent with standard radiological convention.
Locate the mass relative to the great vessels (ascending aorta, superior vena cava) to confirm it is in the anterior mediastinum.
Distinguish the correct side by verifying the mass is on the viewer's left (patient's right), rejecting options that describe the contralateral side despite similar density features.

skill.trigger: When characterizing the internal composition of a mediastinal mass to differentiate between solid, cystic, or calcified lesions.
steps: Inspect the margin of the mass for hyperdense (bright white) areas indicating calcification, specifically looking for a peripheral rim pattern.
Evaluate the central attenuation; distinguish low-density/heterogeneous centers from homogeneous soft-tissue density.
Select the option describing 'calcification' and heterogeneous/low-density center over options describing 'homogeneous density' when a bright rim and dark center are visible.

skill.trigger: When evaluating a chest X-ray for radiological signs of chronic pulmonary embolism or pulmonary hypertension.
steps: Assess the size and contour of the main and hilar pulmonary arteries; look for enlargement (prominence) which suggests elevated pulmonary pressure.
Evaluate the cardiac silhouette, specifically the right heart border and apex, for evidence of right ventricular hypertrophy or enlargement.

Distinguish between options by correlating findings: if pulmonary arteries are normal in caliber and the right ventricle is not enlarged, findings are inconsistent with significant pulmonary hypertension secondary to chronic PE.
